title: Φόνου ἀρχή
about: Odysseus throws off his rags, leaps onto the great threshold of the hall with the bow and a spilled quiver at his feet, and announces a new mark. His first arrow goes through the throat of Antinous as he lifts his golden cup to drink, and the feast is overturned. The suitors, with no weapons within reach, shout at him that he has killed the best young man in Ithaca and will be eaten by vultures, not seeing that their own end is already fastened on them. Odysseus tells them that he has come home, and Eurymachus tries to bargain, blaming Antinous and offering to pay back all that was eaten in bronze and gold. Odysseus refuses any price and gives them a choice between fighting and flight. Eurymachus rallies the suitors and rushes at him, and is shot in the liver. Amphinomus then goes for Odysseus with a sword and is speared from behind by Telemachus, who runs to his father’s side.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ γυμνώθη ῥακέων πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἆλτο δ’ ἐπὶ μέγαν οὐδόν, ἔχων βιὸν ἠδὲ φαρέτρην
ἰῶν ἐμπλείην, ταχέας δ’ ἐκχεύατ’ ὀϊστοὺς
αὐτοῦ πρόσθε ποδῶν, μετὰ δὲ μνηστῆρσιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
But he was stripped bare of the rags, many-wiled Odysseus,
and leapt onto the great threshold, holding the bow and the quiver
of arrows full, and poured out the swift arrows
right before his feet, and among the suitors he said:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles stripped off his rags and leapt onto the great threshold, holding the bow and a quiver full of arrows, and poured the swift arrows out right in front of his feet; and he spoke among the suitors:
sentences.n: γυμνώθη is an aorist passive with the sense of a middle, ‘stripped himself bare’, and ῥακέων is the genitive plural of ῥάκος ‘rag’, saying what he is stripped of. ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’. βιόν is the poetic word for ‘bow’ (the accent separates it from βίος ‘life’), and ἰῶν, the genitive plural of ἰός ‘arrow’, hangs on ἐμπλείην ‘full’. ἐκχεύατ’ is the aorist middle of ἐκχέω ‘pour out’, and ταχέας is ‘swift’. αὐτοῦ is here the adverb ‘right there, on the spot’, not the genitive of αὐτός. μετά with the dative μνηστῆρσιν is ‘among the suitors’, and ἔειπεν is an epic aorist of εἶπον ‘said’. Murray begins a paragraph here, as the disguise comes off.

sentences.t: οὗτος μὲν δὴ ἄεθλος ἀάατος ἐκτετέλεσται·
sentences.l: “This contest indeed, a harmless one, has been completed;
sentences.i: “This contest, which does the suitors no harm, has now been brought to its end;
sentences.n: ἐκτετέλεσται is the perfect passive of ἐκτελέω ‘bring to completion’: ‘has been completed’. ἄεθλος is ‘contest’, the trial of the bow, and οὗτος μὲν δή ‘this, then’ looks forward to νῦν αὖτε in the next lines. The meaning of ἀάατος is not known; ‘harmless’ (the sense ‘not to be harmed’ is also guessed) is the traditional rendering, and the word may be bitterly ironic in Odysseus’ mouth.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖτε σκοπὸν ἄλλον, ὃν οὔ πώ τις βάλεν ἀνήρ,
εἴσομαι, αἴ κε τύχωμι, πόρῃ δέ μοι εὖχος Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.l:
now again another mark, which not yet any man has struck,
I shall find out, if I may hit it, and may Apollo grant me a boast.”
sentences.i: Now again there is another mark, one that no man has yet struck; I shall find out whether I can hit it, and may Apollo grant me the triumph.”
sentences.n: σκοπόν is here the ‘mark’ or target (elsewhere σκοπός is a watcher). ὃν οὔ πώ τις βάλεν ἀνήρ has the unaugmented aorist βάλεν ‘struck’. εἴσομαι is taken as the future of οἶδα, ‘I shall find out’; it could instead be the future of εἶμι ‘go’, ‘I shall go at’, which would take σκοπὸν ἄλλον as a plain accusative of goal, and which is meant is not certain. αἴ κε τύχωμι is ‘if I may hit it’: αἰ is εἰ, κε is the particle that goes with a subjunctive, and τύχωμι is that subjunctive with the epic ending -μι. πόρῃ is a subjunctive used as a wish, ‘may he grant’. εὖχος is ‘boast’, the right to claim a success. The new mark is a man, Antinous, named in the next line.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ ἐπ’ Ἀντινόῳ ἰθύνετο πικρὸν ὀϊστόν.
sentences.l: He spoke, and at Antinous aimed a bitter arrow.
sentences.i: So he said, and aimed a bitter arrow at Antinous.
sentences.n: ἦ καί is ‘he spoke, and’, ἦ being the old verb ‘he said’. ἰθύνετο is the imperfect middle of ἰθύνω ‘make straight, aim’. ἐπ’ Ἀντινόῳ is ‘at Antinous’, and πικρὸν ὀϊστόν is ‘a bitter arrow’, the same adjective as in πικρόγαμοι ‘bitter-wedded’. ὀϊστός is a second word for ‘arrow’, beside ἰός (ἰῶν in line 3), and it is singular here. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὁ καλὸν ἄλεισον ἀναιρήσεσθαι ἔμελλε,
χρύσεον ἄμφωτον, καὶ δὴ μετὰ χερσὶν ἐνώμα,
ὄφρα πίοι οἴνοιο·
sentences.i: He was just about to lift the fine goblet, a golden one with two handles, and was already turning it in his hands, to drink some wine;
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is ‘indeed’ and ὁ is the pronoun ‘he’, Antinous. ἔμελλε with the future infinitive ἀναιρήσεσθαι is ‘was about to take up’. ἄμφωτον, from ἀμφί and οὖς ‘ear’, is ‘two-eared’: a cup with two ear-shaped handles. καὶ δὴ is ‘even then’, and ἐνώμα is the imperfect of νωμάω ‘handle, turn’, with μετὰ χερσίν ‘in his hands’. ὄφρα πίοι is a purpose clause with the optative, and οἴνοιο is a genitive in -οιο (= -ου), ‘some of the wine’; the genitive in -οιο is common in Homer.

sentences.t:
φόνος δέ οἱ οὐκ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
μέμβλετο·
sentences.l:
but slaughter to him in his heart
was not a care;
sentences.i: but slaughter was no care to him in his heart;
sentences.n: μέμβλετο belongs to μέλω ‘be a care to’: a reduplicated past form (from μέμλετο) with an epic β grown between μ and λ. It takes the dative οἱ ‘to him’, and φόνος is ‘slaughter’. Odysseus’ arrow finds a man whose mind is on his drink.

sentences.l:
Who would suppose that among banqueting men
a single man among the many, even if he were very strong,
would contrive for him evil death and black death-fate?
sentences.i: Who would have supposed that among banqueting men, one man alone among so many, however strong he might be, would contrive evil death and the black spirit of death for him?
sentences.n: τίς κ’ οἴοιτο is the potential optative, ‘who would suppose’, and οἴομαι takes an accusative and a future infinitive: μοῦνον ... τεύξειν ‘that a single man will contrive’. δαιτυμόνεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, ‘among banqueting men’; ἐνὶ πλεόνεσσι is ‘among the many’. καὶ εἰ μάλα καρτερὸς εἴη is ‘even if he were very strong’. οἷ is the pronoun ‘for him’, Antinous. κῆρα is the accusative of κήρ ‘death-fate’ (the powers that carry off the dead), not κῆρ ‘heart’; μέλαιναν ‘black’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς κατὰ λαιμὸν ἐπισχόμενος βάλεν ἰῷ,
ἀντικρὺ δ’ ἁπαλοῖο δι’ αὐχένος ἤλυθ’ ἀκωκή.
sentences.l:
Him Odysseus, at the throat taking aim, struck with an arrow,
and straight through the tender neck went the point.
sentences.i: Odysseus took aim at his throat and struck him with an arrow, and the point went straight through his tender neck.
sentences.n: τὸν is a pronoun, ‘him’, Antinous (in Homer ὁ, τόν are pronouns, not an article). Ὀδυσεύς with one σ and Ὀδυσσεύς with two (line 1) are the same name, the doubled σ being a metrical variant. ἐπισχόμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐπέχω, ‘directing (the shaft)’, so ‘taking aim’. βάλεν is unaugmented, and ἰῷ is the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’. ἀντικρύ is ‘straight through’; ἁπαλοῖο is the genitive of ἁπαλός ‘soft, tender’, going with αὐχένος ‘neck’; ἤλυθ’ is the aorist ἤλυθε (Attic ἦλθε), with its augment; ἀκωκή is ‘the point’.

sentences.t:
ἐκλίνθη δ’ ἑτέρωσε, δέπας δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε χειρὸς
βλημένου, αὐτίκα δ’ αὐλὸς ἀνὰ ῥῖνας παχὺς ἦλθεν
αἵματος ἀνδρομέοιο·
sentences.i: He bent over to one side, and the cup dropped from his hand as he was struck, and at once a thick jet of human blood came up through his nostrils;
sentences.n: ἐκλίνθη is the aorist passive of ἐκλίνω ‘bend aside’, and ἑτέρωσε is ‘to the other side’. δέπας ‘cup’ is the goblet of line 9 under its other name. βλημένου, ‘of him struck’, is a genitive picking up the οἱ ‘his’, a common way of saying ‘from the hand of the struck man’. αὐλός is normally a ‘pipe’ or tube; here the blood comes out in a spout or jet. ἀνὰ ῥῖνας is ‘up through the nostrils’. ἀνδρομέοιο is a genitive in -οιο, ‘of a man, human’.

sentences.t:
θοῶς δ’ ἀπὸ εἷο τράπεζαν
ὦσε ποδὶ πλήξας, ἀπὸ δ’ εἴδατα χεῦεν ἔραζε·
sentences.l:
and swiftly away from himself the table
he thrust, striking it with his foot, and the viands he poured out to the ground;
sentences.i: and he quickly shoved the table away from him, striking it with his foot, and spilled the food on the ground;
sentences.n: θοῶς is the adverb ‘swiftly’ (θοός). εἷο is the Homeric genitive of the reflexive pronoun, ‘of himself’, so ‘away from himself’. The first ἀπό goes with εἷο, and ἀπὸ ... χεῦεν is tmesis, a preverb standing apart from its verb: ‘poured away’. ὦσε is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘thrust’; πλήξας, the aorist participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’, with ποδί the dative of means. εἴδατα is the plural of εἶδαρ, a rare word for ‘food’, the dishes on the table; χεῦεν is the unaugmented aorist of χέω ‘pour’; ἔραζε is ‘to the ground’, with the -ζε of direction.

sentences.t: σῖτός τε κρέα τ’ ὀπτὰ φορύνετο.
sentences.l: Food and roast meats were being soiled.
sentences.i: The food and the roast meat were fouled.
sentences.n: φορύνετο is the imperfect passive of φορύνω ‘soil, smear’. The two nouns σῖτος ‘food’ and κρέα ‘meat’ (plural of κρέας), joined by τε ... τε ‘both ... and’, share a singular verb; ὀπτά is ‘roasted’. The sentence about the dying man ends here.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ὁμάδησαν
μνηστῆρες κατὰ δώμαθ’, ὅπως ἴδον ἄνδρα πεσόντα,
ἐκ δὲ θρόνων ἀνόρουσαν ὀρινθέντες κατὰ δῶμα,
πάντοσε παπταίνοντες ἐϋδμήτους ποτὶ τοίχους·
sentences.l:
And they raised an uproar,
the suitors, through the house, when they saw the man fallen,
and from the chairs they sprang up, roused, through the house,
looking about everywhere toward the well-constructed walls;
sentences.i: The suitors raised an uproar through the house when they saw the man fallen, and sprang up from their chairs in alarm all through the house, looking about everywhere toward the well-constructed walls;
sentences.n: τοί is the old form of the pronoun ‘they’, named in the next line as μνηστῆρες. ὁμάδησαν is the aorist of ὁμαδέω ‘make a din’. ὅπως ἴδον is ‘when they saw’ (ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist, Attic εἶδον), and ἄνδρα πεσόντα is ‘the man fallen’. ἀνόρουσαν is the aorist of ἀνορούω ‘spring up’; ὀρινθέντες is the aorist passive participle of ὀρίνω ‘stir up’, ‘thrown into confusion’. πάντοσε is ‘in every direction’, παπταίνοντες ‘glancing about’. ἐϋδμήτους, ‘well-constructed’, is built on ἐύ- and the root of δέμω ‘build’, and ποτί is πρός ‘toward’. They are looking for weapons, as the next line shows.

sentences.t: οὐδέ πη ἀσπὶς ἔην οὐδ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος ἑλέσθαι.
sentences.l: And nowhere was there a shield, nor a sturdy spear, to take.
sentences.i: But there was no shield anywhere, nor a sturdy spear to lay hold of.
sentences.n: οὐδέ πη is ‘and nowhere’ (πη ‘anywhere’ after the negative). ἔην is the uncontracted imperfect of εἰμί, ‘there was’ (Attic ἦν). ἑλέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of αἱρέω, ‘to take up’, an infinitive of purpose after ‘there was’. ἄλκιμον is ‘sturdy’, from ἀλκή ‘might’.

sentences.t: νείκειον δ’ Ὀδυσῆα χολωτοῖσιν ἐπέεσσι·
sentences.l: And they reviled Odysseus with angry words:
sentences.i: And they reviled Odysseus with angry words:
sentences.n: νείκειον is the uncontracted imperfect of νεικέω ‘quarrel with, revile’. Ὀδυσῆα is the accusative of Ὀδυσσεύς with a single σ (the third spelling of the name seen in this passage, beside Ὀδυσεύς and Ὀδυσσεύς, a metrical convenience). χολωτοῖσιν is the dative plural of χολωτός ‘angry’, from χόλος ‘anger’, and ἐπέεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, ‘words’.

sentences.t: ξεῖνε, κακῶς ἀνδρῶν τοξάζεαι·
sentences.l: “Stranger, badly at men you shoot;
sentences.i: “Stranger, you shoot at men to your own harm;
sentences.n: ξεῖνε is the vocative of ξεῖνος ‘stranger’, and here it is scornful: they do not yet know who he is. κακῶς is ‘ill, badly’, here ‘to your own harm’, as the next two sentences show. τοξάζεαι is the uncontracted second person singular of τοξάζομαι ‘shoot with the bow’ (Attic τοξάζῃ), and ἀνδρῶν is a genitive of the object, ‘at men’. The suitors speak in a body, so the speech has no named speaker.

sentences.t:
οὐκέτ’ ἀέθλων
ἄλλων ἀντιάσεις·
sentences.l:
no longer will you meet
with other contests;
sentences.i: you will never again take part in another contest;
sentences.n: οὐκέτ’ is ‘no longer’. ἀέθλων ἄλλων is ‘other contests’, a genitive after ἀντιάσεις ‘you will meet with, take part in’ (ἀντιάω takes the genitive). ἄεθλος, ἆθλον are spellings of one word, ‘contest’. The threat is that this was his last trial.

sentences.t: νῦν τοι σῶς αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος.
sentences.l: now for you sure is steep destruction.
sentences.i: Now steep destruction is certain for you.
sentences.n: τοι is the dative ‘for you’ (σοι). σῶς is the adjective ‘safe, sound’ (from σάος) agreeing with ὄλεθρος, here ‘assured’, so ‘destruction is a sure thing for you’. αἰπύς ‘steep’ is the standing epithet of ὄλεθρος ‘destruction’, here and in lines 43 and 67. There is no verb, ‘is’ being understood.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ δὴ νῦν φῶτα κατέκτανες ὃς μέγ’ ἄριστος
κούρων εἰν Ἰθάκῃ·
sentences.l:
for indeed now a man you have killed who by far the best
of the young men in Ithaca;
sentences.i: for you have now killed a man who was by far the best of the young men in Ithaca;
sentences.n: καὶ γὰρ δή is ‘for indeed’. κατέκτανες is the second person aorist of κτείνω (Attic ἔκτεινας), with the augment present and the stem κτα-. φῶτα is the accusative of φώς ‘man’. μέγ’ ἄριστος is ‘by far the best’ (μέγα intensifies the superlative), and κούρων is the genitive plural of κοῦρος ‘young man’. εἰν is ἐν ‘in’.

sentences.t: τῷ σ’ ἐνθάδε γῦπες ἔδονται.
sentences.l: therefore here vultures will eat you.”
sentences.i: so here the vultures will eat you.”
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘therefore’ (a dative used as an adverb), σ’ is σε ‘you’, and ἐνθάδε ‘here’ has the -δε suffix. γῦπες is ‘vultures’. ἔδονται is the future middle of ἔδω ‘eat’ (Attic ἔδομαι). The threat is a body left unburied.

sentences.t:
ἴσκεν ἕκαστος ἀνήρ, ἐπεὶ ἦ φάσαν οὐκ ἐθέλοντα
ἄνδρα κατακτεῖναι·
sentences.l:
Each man supposed it so, since indeed they said that unwilling
the man he had killed;
sentences.i: So each of them imagined, since they said he had killed the man without wishing to;
sentences.n: ἴσκεν is the imperfect of ἴσκω ‘suppose, say’ (the dictionaries give both senses, and either would fit; ‘suppose’ is taken), ‘was supposing’. ἐπεὶ ἦ φάσαν is ‘since indeed they said’: φάσαν is the unaugmented ἔφασαν, and this ἦ is ‘truly’, not the ἦ ‘he said’ of line 8. οὐκ ἐθέλοντα is ‘unwilling’ and agrees with Odysseus understood, the subject of κατακτεῖναι ‘to have killed’, with ἄνδρα ‘the man’ as its object. Murray begins a paragraph here: the narrator explains what the suitors think.

sentences.t:
τὸ δὲ νήπιοι οὐκ ἐνόησαν,
ὡς δή σφιν καὶ πᾶσιν ὀλέθρου πείρατ’ ἐφῆπτο.
sentences.l:
but this, foolish ones, they did not perceive,
how for them indeed, even for all, of destruction the limits had been fastened on.
sentences.i: But the fools did not realise how the limits of destruction had been fastened upon every one of them.
sentences.n: τὸ δέ is ‘this, however’, the object of ἐνόησαν ‘perceived’ (νοέω). νήπιοι is ‘foolish’, the narrator’s verdict. ὡς δή is ‘how in truth’, and σφιν is the dative ‘for them’ (σφι). πείρατα is the plural of πεῖραρ ‘limit, end’, also used of a rope or cord, so the picture may be of cords tied on; the Greek does not say which. ὀλέθρου is ‘of destruction’, and ἐφῆπτο is the pluperfect passive of ἐφάπτω ‘fasten on’.

sentences.t: τοὺς δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Them then with a scowl looking addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, looking at them with a scowl, spoke to them:
sentences.n: τοὺς δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘them then’: the pronoun τούς is plural, the suitors. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is ‘looking with a scowl’; the ancient explanation of ὑπόδρα is ‘from under the brows’, but the derivation is not certain. προσέφη is the imperfect of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’. πολύμητις is ‘of many wiles’ (μῆτις ‘cunning’), an epithet that comes with the name every time.

sentences.t:
ὦ κύνες, οὔ μ’ ἔτ’ ἐφάσκεθ’ ὑπότροπον οἴκαδ’ ἱκέσθαι
δήμου ἄπο Τρώων, ὅτι μοι κατεκείρετε οἶκον,
δμῳῇσιν δὲ γυναιξὶ παρευνάζεσθε βιαίως,
αὐτοῦ τε ζώοντος ὑπεμνάασθε γυναῖκα,
sentences.l:
“O dogs, you no longer claimed that I would reach home returning
from the land of the Trojans, since you were stripping my house bare,
and with maidservant women you lay by force,
and while I myself was living you wooed my wife underhand,
sentences.i: “You dogs, you claimed that I would never come back home from the land of the Trojans, since you were stripping my house bare, and lying with the maidservants by force, and courting my wife underhand while I myself was alive,
sentences.n: ὦ κύνες is ‘O dogs’, an insult. οὔ μ’ ἔτ’ ἐφάσκεθ’ is ‘you no longer claimed me’: ἐφάσκεθ’ is the imperfect of φάσκω ‘claim’, its τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ὑπότροπον ‘returning’; me ... ἱκέσθαι is accusative and infinitive, ‘that I would reach’. δήμου ἄπο Τρώων is ‘from the land of the Trojans’, ἄπο standing after its noun. κατεκείρετε is the imperfect of κατακείρω ‘shear down, strip bare’. δμῳῇσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν (δμῳή ‘maidservant’); παρευνάζεσθε is ‘you lay beside’ (an imperfect without its augment, which looks like a present). ὑπεμνάασθε is the uncontracted imperfect of ὑπομνάομαι ‘court’, the ὑπο- suggesting underhand dealing. αὐτοῦ ... ζώοντος is a genitive absolute, ‘while I myself was alive’. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
οὔτε θεοὺς δείσαντες, οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν,
οὔτε τιν’ ἀνθρώπων νέμεσιν κατόπισθεν ἔσεσθαι·
sentences.l:
neither fearing the gods, who hold the wide heaven,
nor any resentment of men to come afterwards;
sentences.i: not fearing the gods who hold the wide heaven, and not expecting any resentment from men to come afterwards;
sentences.n: οὔτε ... οὔτε is ‘neither ... nor’. δείσαντες is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’. οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν is ‘who hold the wide heaven’, οἵ being the relative. In the second clause the accusative and future infinitive νέμεσιν ... ἔσεσθαι is ‘that resentment would come’, as if the verb were ‘expecting’ rather than ‘fearing’. νέμεσις is ‘resentment’, the anger of others at a wrong, and κατόπισθεν ‘afterwards’.

sentences.t: νῦν ὑμῖν καὶ πᾶσιν ὀλέθρου πείρατ’ ἐφῆπται.
sentences.l: Now for you, even for all, of destruction the limits have been fastened on.”
sentences.i: Now the limits of destruction have been fastened upon every one of you.”
sentences.n: This is line 33 with the person and tense moved: ἐφῆπτο ‘had been fastened on’ there, ἐφῆπται ‘have been fastened on’ here, the perfect passive. What the narrator said of the suitors’ blindness, Odysseus now says to their faces.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τοὺς δ’ ἄρα πάντας ὑπὸ χλωρὸν δέος εἷλεν·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and them then all beneath pale fear seized;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and pale fear seized them all;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’. τοὺς δ’ ἄρα πάντας is ‘them all’, with ἄρα ‘then’. χλωρόν is ‘pale’ (it also means ‘green, yellow’) and δέος is ‘fear’. εἷλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘seize’; ὑπό is its preverb in tmesis, and its exact force is not clear, ‘seized’ being the sense. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t: πάπτηνεν δὲ ἕκαστος ὅπη φύγοι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.l: and each looked about where he might flee steep destruction.
sentences.i: and each of them looked about for some way to escape steep destruction.
sentences.n: πάπτηνεν is the unaugmented aorist of παπταίνω ‘look about’. ὅπη φύγοι, ‘where he might flee’, is an indirect question with the optative after a past tense, and φεύγω takes the accusative αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον ‘steep destruction’, the phrase of lines 28 and 67.

sentences.t: Εὐρύμαχος δέ μιν οἶος ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.l: But Eurymachus, him, alone, answering addressed:
sentences.i: Eurymachus alone spoke to him in answer:
sentences.n: Εὐρύμαχος has no patronymic here. μιν is the pronoun ‘him’, Odysseus. οἶος is ‘alone’: he alone speaks, since the others are struck with fear. ἀμειβόμενος is ‘answering’ and προσέειπεν ‘addressed’, so this is the answering formula in its two-verb form.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ Ὀδυσεὺς Ἰθακήσιος εἰλήλουθας,
ταῦτα μὲν αἴσιμα εἶπας, ὅσα ῥέζεσκον Ἀχαιοί,
πολλὰ μὲν ἐν μεγάροισιν ἀτάσθαλα, πολλὰ δ’ ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ.
sentences.l:
“If indeed you are Odysseus the Ithacan, come,
these things in due measure you have said, as many as the Achaeans used to do,
many indeed in the halls, wanton deeds, and many in the country.
sentences.i: “If you have indeed come as Odysseus of Ithaca, then you have said what is in due measure about all that the Achaeans used to do: many wanton deeds in the halls, and many in the country.
sentences.n: εἰλήλουθας is the perfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘you have come’ (Attic ἐλήλυθας); the condition is ‘if you really are Odysseus’, which he does not yet know. αἴσιμα εἶπας is ‘you have said what is in due measure’: αἴσιμος is ‘fitting, in due measure’, from αἶσα ‘portion’, and εἶπας is the aorist of λέγω, and the μέν looks forward to ἀλλά in line 48. ὅσα ῥέζεσκον is ‘all that they used to do’: ῥέζεσκον is the iterative imperfect in -σκον of ῥέζω ‘do’. The Achaeans here are the suitors and their kind. ἀτάσθαλα is the neuter plural adjective used as a noun, ‘wanton things’, related to the noun ἀτασθαλίαι of the poem’s opening. ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ is ‘in the country’. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἤδη κεῖται ὃς αἴτιος ἔπλετο πάντων,
Ἀντίνοος·
sentences.l:
But he already lies, who was the cause of all,
Antinous;
sentences.i: But he already lies dead who was the cause of it all, Antinous;
sentences.n: ὁ μέν is the pronoun ‘he’, set against σὺ δέ in line 54, and κεῖται, ‘lies’, is the word for the dead. ὃς αἴτιος ἔπλετο πάντων is ‘who was responsible for all’: ἔπλετο is an old past tense of πέλομαι ‘be, prove’, and αἴτιος takes the genitive. The name is held back to the end of the clause.

sentences.t:
οὗτος γὰρ ἐπίηλεν τάδε ἔργα,
οὔ τι γάμου τόσσον κεχρημένος οὐδὲ χατίζων,
ἀλλ’ ἄλλα φρονέων, τά οἱ οὐκ ἐτέλεσσε Κρονίων,
sentences.i: for it was he who urged on these deeds, not so much in need of a marriage or wishing for one as thinking of other things, which the son of Cronus did not bring to pass for him,
sentences.n: ἐπίηλεν is the aorist of ἐπιϊάλλω ‘send upon’, here ‘urged on’; the verb is rare and the sense comes from the context. οὔ τι γάμου τόσσον is ‘not so much for marriage’; κεχρημένος, the perfect participle of χράομαι ‘need’, and χατίζων ‘lacking, wanting’ both take the genitive γάμου. ἀλλ’ ἄλλα φρονέων is ‘thinking other things’, ‘having other aims in mind’. τά is the relative ‘which’; ἐτέλεσσε is the aorist of τελέω ‘fulfil’ with doubled σ. Κρονίων is ‘the son of Cronus’, Zeus, whom Eurymachus does not name.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ Ἰθάκης κατὰ δῆμον ἐϋκτιμένης βασιλεύοι
αὐτός, ἀτὰρ σὸν παῖδα κατακτείνειε λοχήσας.
sentences.l:
that over the land of well-built Ithaca he might be king
himself, and your son kill, lying in ambush.
sentences.i: so that he himself might be king over the land of well-settled Ithaca, and kill your son from ambush.
sentences.n: ὄφρ’ with the optative βασιλεύοι is a purpose clause, ‘so that he might be king’, and a second optative, κατακτείνειε, is joined to it by ἀτάρ ‘and moreover’. λοχήσας, the aorist participle of λοχάω, is ‘lying in ambush’. ἐϋκτιμένης ‘well-built, well-settled’ is built from ἐύ- and the participle of κτίζω ‘found, settle’, agreeing with Ἰθάκης, and δῆμος is ‘land’. σὸν παῖδα is ‘your son’, Telemachus. These are the dead man’s alleged aims as Eurymachus gives them to Odysseus.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὁ μὲν ἐν μοίρῃ πέφαται, σὺ δὲ φείδεο λαῶν
σῶν·
sentences.l:
But now he in due portion has been slain, and you, spare
your people;
sentences.i: But now he has been killed as was due, and you, spare your own people;
sentences.n: ὁ μέν ... σὺ δέ sets the dead man against Odysseus. ἐν μοίρῃ is ‘in due measure, rightly’, μοῖρα being ‘portion’, and Eurymachus grants that Antinous has had his due share. πέφαται is the perfect passive of φένω ‘slay’, related to φόνος. φείδεο is the imperative of φείδομαι ‘spare’, in the uncontracted -εο form, with the genitive λαῶν σῶν ‘your people’ (λαός ‘people’; σός ‘your’). Here ‘your people’ means the suitors, whom Eurymachus presents as Odysseus’ own subjects.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἄμμες ὄπισθεν ἀρεσσάμενοι κατὰ δῆμον,
ὅσσα τοι ἐκπέποται καὶ ἐδήδοται ἐν μεγάροισι,
τιμὴν ἀμφὶς ἄγοντες ἐεικοσάβοιον ἕκαστος,
χαλκόν τε χρυσόν τ’ ἀποδώσομεν,
sentences.l:
but we afterwards, having made amends throughout the land
for as much as has been drunk up and eaten up from you in the halls,
each one bringing separately a compensation worth twenty oxen,
bronze and gold will pay back,
sentences.i: but we, afterwards, shall make amends through the land for all that has been drunk and eaten in your halls, each of us bringing a compensation worth twenty oxen, and pay you back in bronze and gold,
sentences.n: ἄμμες is the epic form of ἡμεῖς ‘we’, and ὄπισθεν is ‘afterwards’. ἀρεσσάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἀρέσκω ‘satisfy’, ‘having made amends’, with κατὰ δῆμον ‘through the land’: the sense may be that they will collect the payment from the people, but the Greek does not say so. ὅσσα τοι ἐκπέποται καὶ ἐδήδοται is ‘as much as has been drunk up and eaten up at your cost’ (τοι is ‘to you’): both are perfect passives, of ἐκπίνω and ἔδω. τιμήν here is ‘compensation’, ἀμφίς ‘separately, each for himself’, and ἐεικοσάβοιον ‘worth twenty oxen’, oxen being a unit of value. ἀποδώσομεν is the future of ἀποδίδωμι ‘pay back’. The sentence continues in the next unit.

sentences.t:
εἰς ὅ κε σὸν κῆρ
ἰανθῇ·
sentences.l:
until your heart
be warmed;
sentences.i: until your heart is softened;
sentences.n: εἰς ὅ κε is ‘until’ (literally ‘up to the point that’), with the aorist subjunctive passive ἰανθῇ of ἰαίνω ‘warm, cheer, soften’. σὸν κῆρ is ‘your heart’: κῆρ is the heart, not κήρ ‘death-fate’.

sentences.t: πρὶν δ’ οὔ τι νεμεσσητὸν κεχολῶσθαι.
sentences.l: and before that it is not at all a thing to be resented to have been angry.”
sentences.i: Until then no one can resent your anger.”
sentences.n: πρὶν δέ is ‘but before that’. νεμεσσητόν is the verbal adjective of νεμεσάω ‘feel resentment at’, so ‘a thing to be resented’ or blamed, with οὔ τι ‘not at all’ and ‘is’ understood. κεχολῶσθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of χολόω ‘make angry’, ‘to have been angered’, so ‘to be angry’. Eurymachus ends on a concession.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, Eurymachus; the singular of the formula of line 34. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is ‘looking with a scowl’ (the derivation of ὑπόδρα is not certain), προσέφη is the imperfect ‘addressed’, and πολύμητις is ‘of many wiles’. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύμαχ’, οὐδ’ εἴ μοι πατρώϊα πάντ’ ἀποδοῖτε,
ὅσσα τε νῦν ὔμμ’ ἐστὶ καὶ εἴ ποθεν ἄλλ’ ἐπιθεῖτε,
οὐδέ κεν ὣς ἔτι χεῖρας ἐμὰς λήξαιμι φόνοιο
πρὶν πᾶσαν μνηστῆρας ὑπερβασίην ἀποτῖσαι.
sentences.l:
“Eurymachus, not even if my father’s goods all you gave back,
as many as now to you are, and if from anywhere else you added,
not even so would I still hold my hands from slaughter
before the suitors all their overstepping pay back.
sentences.i: “Eurymachus, not even if you gave me back everything that was my father’s, all that you now have, and added more from some other source, not even so would I hold my hands back from slaughter before the suitors had paid in full for all their transgression.
sentences.n: Εὐρύμαχ’ is the vocative with its final vowel elided. οὐδ’ εἴ ... ἀποδοῖτε is a remote condition, ‘not even if you were to give back’, with the aorist optative of ἀποδίδωμι. πατρώϊα are ‘things of one’s father’, here his father’s goods. ὔμμ’ is the elided epic dative ὔμμι ‘to you’ (ὑμῖν), so ὅσσα τε νῦν ὔμμ’ ἐστί is ‘as much as you now have’. ἐπιθεῖτε is the aorist optative of ἐπιτίθημι ‘add’. οὐδέ κεν ὣς ... λήξαιμι is ‘not even so would I stop’, with the accented ὥς ‘so’; λήγω takes the genitive φόνοιο ‘from slaughter’, and here χεῖρας ἐμάς is its object, ‘make my hands stop’. ὑπερβασίην is ‘overstepping’, the going beyond what is allowed, and ἀποτῖσαι is ‘to pay back’.

sentences.t:
νῦν ὑμῖν παράκειται ἐναντίον ἠὲ μάχεσθαι
ἢ φεύγειν, ὅς κεν θάνατον καὶ κῆρας ἀλύξῃ·
sentences.l:
Now to you lies at hand face to face either to fight
or to flee, whoever may escape death and the death-fates;
sentences.i: Now it lies with you either to fight me face to face or to run, if any of you is to escape death and the spirits of death;
sentences.n: παράκειται is ‘lies at hand’, here ‘is open to you’. ἠέ ... ἤ is ‘either ... or’, with the infinitives μάχεσθαι and φεύγειν, and ἐναντίον ‘face to face’ goes with the first. ὅς κεν ... ἀλύξῃ is an indefinite relative clause with κε and the aorist subjunctive of ἀλύσκω: ‘whoever may escape’. κῆρας is the plural of κήρ, the ‘death-fates’, not κῆρ ‘heart’.

sentences.t: ἀλλά τιν’ οὐ φεύξεσθαι ὀΐομαι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.l: but anyone to escape not, I think, steep destruction.”
sentences.i: but I do not think any of you will escape steep destruction.”
sentences.n: ὀΐομαι is ‘I think’, followed by τιν’ οὐ φεύξεσθαι, an accusative and future infinitive with οὐ: ‘that no one will escape’, which answers the ὅς κεν ἀλύξῃ of the line before. αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον is the phrase of lines 28 and 43.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῶν δ’ αὐτοῦ λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and of them on the spot were loosed the knees and the dear heart.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and their knees gave way on the spot, and their hearts too.
sentences.n: τῶν is ‘of them’, a genitive of possession with γούνατα ‘knees’ and ἦτορ ‘heart’. αὐτοῦ is ‘right there, on the spot’. λύτο is the unaugmented aorist of λύω, in the middle form with passive sense, ‘were loosed’. The loosened knees and heart are Homer’s picture of strength failing; φίλον ‘dear’ is almost ‘own’. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Εὐρύμαχος προσεφώνεε δεύτερον αὖτις·
sentences.l: And to them Eurymachus spoke again, a second time:
sentences.i: Eurymachus spoke to them again, for the second time:
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, ‘to them’. προσεφώνεε is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’. δεύτερον αὖτις is ‘a second time again’: he has spoken once already, at line 44.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐ γὰρ σχήσει ἀνὴρ ὅδε χεῖρας ἀάπτους,
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ ἔλλαβε τόξον ἐΰξοον ἠδὲ φαρέτρην,
οὐδοῦ ἄπο ξεστοῦ τοξάσσεται, εἰς ὅ κε πάντας
ἄμμε κατακτείνῃ·
sentences.l:
“Friends, for this man will not hold back his untouchable hands,
but since he has taken the well-polished bow and the quiver,
from the polished threshold he will shoot, until all of us
he kills;
sentences.i: “Friends, this man will not hold back his irresistible hands; now that he has taken up the well-polished bow and the quiver, he will shoot from the polished threshold until he has killed every one of us;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is ‘friends’. σχήσει is the future of ἔχω ‘hold back’. The meaning of ἀάπτους, said of hands, is not known: ‘untouchable’ and ‘irresistible’ are the traditional guesses. ἐΰξοον is ‘well-polished’ (ἐυ- and ξέω ‘plane, polish’), and ξεστοῦ ‘polished’ is the same root. ἔλλαβε is ἔλαβε with doubled λ, ‘has taken’; οὐδοῦ ἄπο is ‘from the threshold’, and τοξάσσεται is the future middle of τοξάζομαι ‘shoot’. εἰς ὅ κε with the aorist subjunctive κατακτείνῃ is ‘until he has killed’, ἄμμε (the epic accusative of ἡμεῖς) being ‘us’. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μνησώμεθα χάρμης.
sentences.l: but let us bethink ourselves of battle.
sentences.i: so let us turn our thoughts to fighting.
sentences.n: ἀλλά is here ‘so, then’. μνησώμεθα is a hortatory aorist subjunctive middle of μιμνήσκομαι, ‘let us bethink ourselves of’, with the genitive χάρμης ‘battle’; χάρμη is an old word for the joy or fury of fighting.

sentences.t:
φάσγανά τε σπάσσασθε καὶ ἀντίσχεσθε τραπέζας
ἰῶν ὠκυμόρων·
sentences.l:
draw your swords, and hold up the tables
against the swift-doomed arrows;
sentences.i: draw your swords, and hold the tables up against the arrows that bring a swift doom;
sentences.n: σπάσσασθε is the aorist middle imperative of σπάω ‘draw’, and φάσγανα is ‘swords’. ἀντίσχεσθε is the imperative middle of ἀντέχω ‘hold up against’, with the genitive ἰῶν ὠκυμόρων ‘against the swift-doomed arrows’; ὠκύμορος is built on ὠκύς ‘swift’ and μόρος ‘doom’, and of arrows it means that they bring a swift doom. The tables serve as shields, since there is no shield to hand.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δ’ αὐτῷ πάντες ἔχωμεν
ἀθρόοι, εἴ κέ μιν οὐδοῦ ἀπώσομεν ἠδὲ θυράων,
ἔλθωμεν δ’ ἀνὰ ἄστυ, βοὴ δ’ ὤκιστα γένοιτο·
sentences.i: and let us all press upon him together in a mass, to see whether we can thrust him from the threshold and the doors, and go up through the town, so that the shout goes up as fast as possible;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ ... ἔχωμεν is a hortatory subjunctive of ἐπέχω ‘press upon’, with ἐπί apart from its verb (tmesis) and αὐτῷ ‘him’. ἀθρόοι is ‘massed together’. εἴ κέ μιν ... ἀπώσομεν is ‘in case we can thrust him back’, a hopeful ‘if’ with κε and a short-vowel subjunctive (ἀπώσομεν could also be read as a future), with οὐδοῦ ... θυράων ‘from the threshold and the doors’. ἔλθωμεν δ’ ἀνὰ ἄστυ is ‘and let us go up through the town’ (ἀνά with the accusative), and βοή is the ‘shout’ that will raise an alarm. ὤκιστα is the superlative of the adverb ὠκύς, ‘as fast as possible’, and γένοιτο is the aorist optative as a wish.

sentences.t: τῷ κε τάχ’ οὗτος ἀνὴρ νῦν ὕστατα τοξάσσαιτο.
sentences.l: then soon this man now for the last time would shoot.”
sentences.i: and then this man would soon be shooting for the last time.”
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘in that case, by that means’. κε with the optative τοξάσσαιτο gives a potential, ‘would shoot’. τάχ’ is τάχα ‘soon’, and ὕστατα, the neuter plural of the superlative ὕστατος used as an adverb, is ‘for the last time’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας εἰρύσσατο φάσγανον ὀξὺ
χάλκεον, ἀμφοτέρωθεν ἀκαχμένον, ἆλτο δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ
σμερδαλέα ἰάχων·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and drew his sharp bronze sword, sharpened on both sides, and leapt at Odysseus with a frightful shout;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is ‘so then having spoken’. εἰρύσσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, and φάσγανον ὀξύ is ‘the sharp sword’. χάλκεον is ‘of bronze’. ἀκαχμένον is related to ἀκή and ἀκωκή ‘point’, so ‘pointed’ or ‘sharpened’, and ἀμφοτέρωθεν ‘from both sides’ shows the sword is edged on both. ἆλτο is the verb of line 2, now with ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘at him’. σμερδαλέα is the neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘frightfully’, and ἰάχων is the participle of ἰάχω ‘cry out’. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἁμαρτῆ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἰὸν ἀποπροίει, βάλε δὲ στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν,
ἐν δέ οἱ ἥπατι πῆξε θοὸν βέλος·
sentences.i: At the same instant heavenly Odysseus let fly an arrow and struck him in the chest beside the breast, and fixed the swift shaft in his liver;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is Odysseus, with δῖος ‘heavenly’, the stock epithet. ἁμαρτῇ is ‘at the same moment’ (an adverb, literally ‘together’). ἰὸν ἀποπροίει is ‘sent an arrow off’, the imperfect of ἀποπροΐημι. βάλε is unaugmented, and στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν is ‘the chest beside the breast’, μαζός being the breast or nipple. πῆξε is the aorist of πήγνυμι ‘fix’, and ἧπαρ (here ἥπατι) is ‘liver’; θοὸν βέλος is ‘the swift shaft’. The pronoun οἱ ‘in him’ stands before the noun ἥπατι, ‘in his liver’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄρα χειρὸς
φάσγανον ἧκε χαμᾶζε, περιρρηδὴς δὲ τραπέζῃ
κάππεσεν ἰδνωθείς, ἀπὸ δ’ εἴδατα χεῦεν ἔραζε
καὶ δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον·
sentences.l:
and out of his hand
the sword he let fall to the ground, and sprawling over the table
he fell, doubled over, and the viands he poured out to the ground
and the double cup;
sentences.i: and he let the sword fall from his hand to the ground, and, doubled over, fell sprawling across the table, and spilled the food on the ground, and the double cup;
sentences.n: ἐκ ... ἧκε is tmesis for ἐξῆκε, the aorist of ἵημι ‘let go, let fall’; χαμᾶζε is ‘to the ground’ with the -ζε of direction. περιρρηδής is a rare word, ‘sprawling over’, the sense being taken from the context. κάππεσεν is κατέπεσεν, ‘fell down’, with the final consonant of the preverb assimilated; ἰδνωθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἰδνόω ‘double up’. ἀπὸ δ’ εἴδατα χεῦεν ἔραζε repeats the words of line 20. δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον is ‘the double cup’ (the sense of ἀμφικύπελλον is disputed, ‘double’ or ‘two-handled’); it hangs on the same verb χεῦεν, so he spilled the food and the cup alike.

sentences.t:
ὁ δὲ χθόνα τύπτε μετώπῳ
θυμῷ ἀνιάζων, ποσὶ δὲ θρόνον ἀμφοτέροισι
λακτίζων ἐτίνασσε·
sentences.i: and he beat the ground with his forehead in anguish of heart, and kicked at the chair with both feet and shook it;
sentences.n: ὁ δέ is Eurymachus. χθόνα is the accusative of χθών ‘earth’, and μετώπῳ ‘with his forehead’ is a dative of means. θυμῷ ἀνιάζων is ‘distressed in his heart’ (ἀνιάζω ‘be in distress’); this is the dying man’s agony. ποσί ‘with feet’ is a dative plural, with ἀμφοτέροισι ‘both’; λακτίζων is ‘kicking’, and ἐτίνασσε, the imperfect of τινάσσω, is ‘kept shaking’.

sentences.t: κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν δ’ ἔχυτ’ ἀχλύς.
sentences.l: and down over his eyes was poured a haze.
sentences.i: and a haze poured down over his eyes.
sentences.n: κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν is ‘down over his eyes’ (κατά with the genitive). ἔχυτ’ is ἔχυτο, the aorist middle of χέω ‘pour’ with its augment, here with a passive sense. ἀχλύς is ‘haze, mist’, the darkening that comes with death, and is the subject.

sentences.t:
Ἀμφίνομος δ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἐείσατο κυδαλίμοιο
ἀντίος ἀΐξας, εἴρυτο δὲ φάσγανον ὀξύ,
εἴ πώς οἱ εἴξειε θυράων.
sentences.l:
And Amphinomus made for Odysseus, glorious,
rushing straight at him, and had drawn his sharp sword,
if in any way he would give way to him from the doors.
sentences.i: Amphinomus made for glorious Odysseus, rushing straight at him with his sharp sword drawn, in the hope that Odysseus would somehow give way to him and leave the doors.
sentences.n: ἐείσατο is the aorist of ἵεμαι ‘rush’, with the genitive Ὀδυσῆος, ‘at Odysseus’; Ὀδυσῆος is the Homeric genitive of Ὀδυσσεύς, and κυδαλίμοιο is a genitive in -οιο. ἀντίος is ‘facing, straight at’, with ἀΐξας, the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’. εἴρυτο is a pluperfect of ἐρύω ‘draw’, ‘had drawn’. εἴ πώς οἱ εἴξειε θυράων is ‘in the hope that somehow he would give way to him from the doors’: εἰ with the optative expresses the hope, εἴκω is ‘yield’, οἱ is ‘to him’ (Amphinomus), and θυράων is a genitive of separation. The subject of εἴξειε is Odysseus. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄρα μιν φθῆ
Τηλέμαχος κατόπισθε βαλὼν χαλκήρεϊ δουρὶ
ὤμων μεσσηγύς, διὰ δὲ στήθεσφιν ἔλασσεν·
sentences.i: But Telemachus forestalled him, striking from behind with a bronze-fitted spear between the shoulders, and drove it through his chest;
sentences.n: φθῆ is the unaugmented aorist of φθάνω ‘get in first’, with the accusative μιν ‘him’. κατόπισθε is ‘from behind’. χαλκήρεϊ is the dative of χαλκήρης ‘bronze-fitted’ (from the root of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’), going with δουρί ‘spear’. ὤμων μεσσηγύς is ‘between the shoulders’. διὰ ... ἔλασσεν is tmesis, from ἐλαύνω ‘drive’; στήθεσφιν has the old ending -φιν, here ‘through the chest’.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, χθόνα δ’ ἤλασε παντὶ μετώπῳ.
sentences.l: He fell with a thud, and struck the earth with his whole forehead.
sentences.i: He fell with a thud and struck the ground with all of his forehead.
sentences.n: δούπησεν is the aorist of δουπέω ‘thud’, from δοῦπος, a heavy crash, and πεσών is the aorist participle of πίπτω ‘fall’. The subject, Amphinomus, is not named. χθόνα δ’ ἤλασε παντὶ μετώπῳ is ‘struck the earth with his whole forehead’, and ἤλασε is the aorist of the same verb ἐλαύνω as ἔλασσεν in the line before. It echoes the end of Eurymachus in lines 86 to 88.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἀπόρουσε, λιπὼν δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος
αὐτοῦ ἐν Ἀμφινόμῳ·
sentences.l:
And Telemachus sprang away, leaving his long-shadowed spear
there in Amphinomus;
sentences.i: Telemachus sprang away, leaving his long-shadowed spear there in Amphinomus;
sentences.n: ἀπόρουσε is the aorist of ἀπορούω ‘spring away’, and λιπών is ‘leaving’. δολιχόσκιον is ‘long-shadowed’, from δολιχός ‘long’ and σκιά ‘shadow’; the likely sense is that the spear throws a long shadow, that is, has a long shaft. ἔγχος is ‘spear’. αὐτοῦ is ‘right there’, and ἐν Ἀμφινόμῳ is ‘in Amphinomus’, the spear being left in the body.

sentences.t:
περὶ γὰρ δίε μή τις Ἀχαιῶν
ἔγχος ἀνελκόμενον δολιχόσκιον ἢ ἐλάσειε
φασγάνῳ ἀΐξας ἠὲ προπρηνέα τύψας.
sentences.l:
for he feared exceedingly lest any of the Achaeans
him pulling out the long-shadowed spear either stab
with a sword, rushing at him, or strike him bent forward.
sentences.i: for he was greatly afraid that, as he pulled out the long-shadowed spear, one of the Achaeans might rush at him and stab him with a sword, or strike him as he bent forward.
sentences.n: περὶ ... δίε is tmesis for περιδίε, ‘was greatly afraid’, from δείδω, with an unaugmented past tense. μή with the optative introduces what is feared: μή τις ... ἐλάσειε ‘lest someone stab’. ἀνελκόμενον is the present middle participle of ἀνέλκω ‘draw up’, taken as masculine accusative because it describes Telemachus, who is the unexpressed object of the verbs, with ἔγχος as its object (the same form could also agree with ἔγχος). ἐλάσειε is the aorist optative of ἐλαύνω, here ‘drive (a blade at), stab’. ἢ ... ἠέ is ‘either ... or’, φασγάνῳ is a dative of means, ἀΐξας is ‘rushing’, and προπρηνέα is ‘bent forward’, likewise accusative for the unexpressed him; τύψας is the aorist participle of τύπτω ‘strike’. Ἀχαιῶν is a partitive genitive with τις, the suitors again.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ θέειν, μάλα δ’ ὦκα φίλον πατέρ’ εἰσαφίκανεν,
ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
He set out to run, and very swiftly his dear father he reached,
and standing close by, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: He set off at a run and very quickly reached his dear father, and, standing close beside him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: βῆ δὲ θέειν is ‘he set out to run’: βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘go’, and θέειν is the uncontracted infinitive of θέω ‘run’ (Attic θεῖν). μάλα δ’ ὦκα is ‘very swiftly’ (ὦκα, adverb of ὠκύς), and φίλον πατέρ’ is ‘his dear father’. εἰσαφίκανεν is the imperfect of εἰσαφικάνω ‘come to, reach’. The second line is the standing formula that introduces a speech: ἱστάμενος ‘standing’, ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’, προσηύδα ‘spoke to’. The words themselves come after the end of this passage.
